title: Northwind x Redwood - reference program intro (design partner + case study)
summary: Intro call to confirm Northwind’s interest in joining Redwood’s customer reference program (design partner). Discussed what participation entails (1–2 reference calls/month, public case study with logo/quotes/optional metrics), constraints around what Northwind can share publicly, and a proposed story angle focused on Dedicated capacity + routing/fallback policies + cost controls. Agreed to schedule a longer customer story interview and begin the logo/quote consent workflow with a defined review window.
topics: What the Redwood reference program is and what we’re asking Northwind to do
Northwind comfort level: logo, quotes, architecture diagram, metrics (exact vs ranges)
Story angle: Dedicated capacity, smart routing/fallback, reliability during peak traffic
Process: draft -> technical validation -> legal/brand approval -> publish
Scheduling the full interview and identifying the right reviewers on Northwind side
questions: Are you comfortable being a reference call for late-stage Dedicated/Private prospects (and how many per month is reasonable)?
Can we use the Northwind logo publicly on the case study page and in sales decks?
Can we include performance/cost outcomes as ranges (e.g., “~30–40% lower $/1M tokens”) vs exact numbers?
Who needs to review/approve externally (legal, brand, comms), and what’s a typical turnaround time?
Are there specific claims you do NOT want us to make publicly (providers used before, exact incident details, volumes)?
next_steps: Redwood (Camila) to send the consent form draft + a one-page overview of the program and examples of published stories.
Redwood (Avery/Markus) to propose 2–3 interview times for a 60-minute customer story interview next week.
Northwind (Priya) to confirm who on their side must approve logo usage and any public metrics (brand/comms/legal contact).
Redwood (Markus) to share a lightweight architecture diagram template and confirm what level of detail is safe to publish.
Northwind (Daniel) to sanity-check a short list of measurable outcomes they’re comfortable sharing as ranges (latency, cost, reliability).
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Date: 2025-10-03
Time: 3:02pm–3:44pm PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Title: Northwind x Redwood - reference program intro (design partner + case study)
Attendees:
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference, Enterprise AE)
- Camila Reyes (Redwood Inference, VP Marketing)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Priya Shah (Northwind Commerce, VP Engineering)
- Daniel Cho (Northwind Commerce, ML Lead)

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Hey Priya, hey Daniel. Good to see you both. I know we’ve got a tight 30, 40 minutes. Um, thanks for making time.

[00:08] Priya Shah: Yeah, no problem. We can do 40. Daniel’s here too.

[00:12] Daniel Cho: Hey everyone.

[00:13] Camila Reyes: Hi Priya, hi Daniel. Camila here. Thanks for hopping on.

[00:17] Markus Klein: Hey folks, Markus. Good to meet you, Daniel.

[00:22] Avery Johnson: Cool. So the goal today is pretty simple. We’re launching a customer reference program—like, a small design partner cohort—three to five customers total. And Northwind is top of our list because your Dedicated rollout has been, honestly, one of the cleaner ones.

[00:40] Avery Johnson: What we want to cover is: what participation would look like, what you’re comfortable sharing publicly, and then if it’s a yes-ish, we schedule a longer interview to actually capture the story.

[00:53] Priya Shah: Okay. And when you say “design partner,” that’s like product feedback, or marketing, or both?

[01:00] Camila Reyes: Great question—more the marketing/reference side. Not “you have to build with beta features” unless you want. The program is basically: (1) a public case study—logo, a couple of quotes, and optional metrics—and (2) being available for reference calls with other prospects, but we put guardrails around that so you’re not swamped.

[01:22] Priya Shah: Got it.

[01:24] Daniel Cho: And the reference calls would be with other e-comm folks or anyone?

[01:29] Avery Johnson: Ideally similar profile—production traffic, latency-sensitive, cares about unit cost. It might be enterprise SaaS too, but we’d brief you, and we’d do it only when it’s a legit late-stage deal.

[01:42] Camila Reyes: And we can set a cap. Like “no more than 1–2 per month,” plus a cooldown if it gets annoying. We’ve seen programs go sideways when it’s ad hoc.

[01:53] Priya Shah: Yeah, I appreciate that. We’ve done references before and it got… kind of out of hand.

[01:59] Avery Johnson: Totally. That’s exactly what we’re trying to avoid.

[02:03] Markus Klein: Also, we’d prep you. Not in a scripted way, but like: what to emphasize, what to avoid, and what questions tend to come up—SLA, reliability, fallbacks, cost per million tokens, that kind of thing.

[02:18] Priya Shah: Okay. So what’s the “public” part? Is it like a blog post?

[02:23] Camila Reyes: It would live on our Case Studies page and we can repurpose as a one-pager PDF for Sales. It’s not a super fluffy blog—more “problem, constraints, solution, implementation, results.” Developer-first tone.

[02:39] Camila Reyes: And you’d get to review it. We have a standard review window—usually 7 to 10 business days—before anything goes live.

[02:49] Daniel Cho: What kind of details are you trying to get into? Because we can’t publish like, exact volumes.

[02:56] Avery Johnson: Yeah, that’s the big thing we wanted to ask. For Northwind we think the story angle is: you moved to Dedicated for predictable throughput during peak, you’re using routing policies so if one model or region is constrained you have fallback, and then you used caching/batching to keep cost sane.

[03:17] Markus Klein: Plus the whole “we can keep the app up even if capacity is tight” thing. That’s actually a strong differentiator.

[03:23] Priya Shah: I’m open to the angle. But we’d need to be careful about saying “fallback” because that implies there were failures.

[03:30] Markus Klein: Totally fair. We can frame it as resilience. Like: “policy-based routing and automatic fallback to maintain SLOs.” Not “we were down.”

[03:43] Camila Reyes: And we don’t have to mention incident-y stuff. It can be proactive architecture.

[03:48] Daniel Cho: What’s the minimum you need for metrics? Like, if we can’t do exact dollars.

[03:55] Camila Reyes: Minimum is actually not numbers. A quote like “we improved latency and got more predictable costs” can be enough. But numbers make it stronger, so we often do ranges.

[04:07] Camila Reyes: Example: “p95 latency improved by ~20–30%,” or “reduced per-token cost by ~X%,” and then we add a disclaimer: “results vary, measured in their environment.”

[04:18] Priya Shah: Ranges are probably okay. No absolute spend, no total request volume.

[04:23] Avery Johnson: That’s consistent with what other customers do.

[04:26] Daniel Cho: Also we’d rather not name previous vendors. Like we evaluated Bedrock and Together and a couple others, but I don’t want that in writing.

[04:34] Camila Reyes: We can avoid naming competitors. Sometimes it’s helpful to say “previous provider” or “managed endpoint,” but we can keep it generic.

[04:43] Markus Klein: We can also keep the architecture diagram abstract. Like boxes for “Redwood Dedicated,” “App backend,” “Observability,” and not include internal service names.

[04:54] Priya Shah: Yeah, I’d want that. No internal naming.

[04:58] Avery Johnson: Makes sense.

[05:01] Camila Reyes: Let me zoom out for 30 seconds on process. If you say yes, we do: (1) a longer interview—usually 60 minutes—with you and whoever is most in the weeds, (2) we draft, (3) Markus or someone does a technical accuracy review, (4) we send it to you for review + legal/brand approval, (5) publish.

[05:26] Priya Shah: Okay.

[05:28] Avery Johnson: And incentives—because it is time—there are a few options. We can do like a conference sponsorship credit, or extended Optimize trial, or a charitable donation. We’re still finalizing, but we can align on what’s meaningful.

[05:45] Priya Shah: I don’t think we can accept like gifts. Donation might be fine. Or credits, but we’d have to run it by finance.

[05:53] Camila Reyes: Yep, we can do a donation option, and we can keep it clean from a compliance perspective.

[06:00] Daniel Cho: Quick question: when you say “Optimize,” that’s the thing that suggests batching and caching config, right?

[06:06] Markus Klein: Yeah. It’s basically the cost/perf toolkit. Not magic, but it helps you tune continuous batching, cache hit rate, and flags regressions.

[06:16] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[06:18] Avery Johnson: So, what are the constraints for Northwind on a public story? Logo is usually the gating item.

[06:25] Priya Shah: Logo might be doable, but it’s not just me. We have a brand team. And legal sometimes wants to review anything that looks like an endorsement.

[06:35] Camila Reyes: That’s normal. Do you know who the approver is?

[06:38] Priya Shah: I can find out. It’s probably someone in comms.

[06:43] Daniel Cho: And also, no screenshots of our UI, obviously.

[06:47] Camila Reyes: Totally. We don’t need screenshots.

[06:50] Markus Klein: On the technical side, what’s safe: “Dedicated capacity in [region],” “policy-based routing,” “prefix caching,” “rate limiting,” “observability.” Anything you’d rather not mention?

[07:04] Priya Shah: Region is okay if it’s just “US.” Don’t put specific availability zones or anything.

[07:10] Markus Klein: Yeah we wouldn’t.

[07:12] Daniel Cho: Also avoid details on our fraud models. That’s separate.

[07:16] Avery Johnson: Yep. We’d keep it focused on your customer-facing assistant and search/chat experience.

[07:22] Priya Shah: Right.

[07:24] Camila Reyes: What about describing the use case? “Ecommerce search + shopping assistant” is fine?

[07:28] Priya Shah: That’s fine.

[07:30] Daniel Cho: Yeah.

[07:32] Avery Johnson: Great. So story angle—just sanity check—when we think of Northwind, we think: peak season traffic, needing predictable throughput, and making sure if a model gets slow you don’t blow your p95 budget.

[07:47] Priya Shah: That’s accurate. We basically couldn’t have variable performance. The business freaks out if checkout questions lag.

[07:55] Markus Klein: Totally. And that’s where dedicated pools + routing rules matter.

[07:59] Daniel Cho: What exactly would you say about fallback? Because we do have a primary and then a smaller model as backup, but we don’t want to say which one.

[08:08] Markus Klein: We can say “compatible model variants.” Or “smaller variant.” No model names. And we can frame it as “automatic fallback when SLOs are at risk.”

[08:21] Camila Reyes: Also we can keep it at the policy layer: “If latency exceeds threshold, route to alternate.” No need to name providers or model IDs.

[08:31] Priya Shah: Okay.

[08:32] Avery Johnson: On metrics: do you have anything you’d be comfortable with as a range? Like, you had an internal goal for p95, and after tuning you hit it.

[08:43] Daniel Cho: We do. I can share ranges in the interview. Like pre/post. But it has to be “in our tests” and not a guarantee.

[08:52] Camila Reyes: Perfect. We have standard disclaimer language.

[08:55] Priya Shah: I’d prefer no exact uptime numbers, though.

[08:59] Avery Johnson: That’s fine. We can say “improved reliability” or “fewer timeouts.”

[09:04] Markus Klein: Or “more predictable tail latency.” That’s often better than uptime claims anyway.

[09:09] Daniel Cho: Yeah, tail latency is the story.

[09:12] Camila Reyes: Great.

[09:14] Avery Johnson: Logistics-wise: we’d love to do the full interview next week if possible. And we’d like to target publishing… late October or early November? That’s flexible depending on your approvals.

[09:29] Priya Shah: Early November is more realistic. October gets busy on our end.

[09:34] Camila Reyes: Okay. We can aim for a draft to you by, say, end of October, then publish after review.

[09:42] Avery Johnson: That works.

[09:44] Markus Klein: For the interview, who should join? Priya you, Daniel you, and maybe someone on infra? Whoever did the dedicated sizing.

[09:53] Priya Shah: We can bring Alex from platform. But I need to check his schedule.

[09:58] Daniel Cho: I can handle most of the ML side.

[10:01] Avery Johnson: Great.

[10:02] Camila Reyes: We keep it conversational. We’ll ask about the before state, constraints, why Dedicated, and then implementation details at a high level.

[10:12] Priya Shah: Okay.

[10:14] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk guardrails for reference calls too. If we do this, what’s a reasonable cap? You said you’ve been burned before.

[10:23] Priya Shah: I’d say one per month to start. And if it’s a big deal, maybe two, but not consistently.

[10:31] Camila Reyes: That’s totally fine. We can codify “max 1–2 per month, by approval.”

[10:37] Markus Klein: And we’ll always route requests through your point person, not randomly emailing Daniel at 10pm.

[10:43] Daniel Cho: Thank you.

[10:45] Avery Johnson: Also, if there’s a topic you don’t want to talk about—like internal tooling, or pricing—you can just say “I can’t comment.” And we’ll tell prospects that up front.

[10:56] Priya Shah: Yeah. Pricing we won’t discuss.

[10:59] Camila Reyes: Totally standard.

[11:02] Avery Johnson: Cool. Any concerns about legal? We have a consent form that covers logo, quotes, and what type of metrics you approve for publication.

[11:12] Priya Shah: We’ll need to see it. Legal will want a revocation clause probably.

[11:18] Camila Reyes: It has that. Like you can revoke with written notice, and we stop using the assets going forward.

[11:24] Daniel Cho: And how do you handle quote approvals? Because sometimes marketing edits a quote and it becomes… not what we said.

[11:31] Camila Reyes: Yep. We’ll send the exact quote we want to attribute, you can edit it for accuracy, and we won’t publish until you sign off. We can also attribute by name/title or by “VP Engineering” if you prefer, though name is stronger.

[11:47] Priya Shah: Name might be okay. I’m fine with that if the quote is accurate.

[11:52] Avery Johnson: Great.

[11:54] Markus Klein: On the technical claims, we also do an internal proof pass. Like if we say “prefix caching,” we confirm you actually used it. No marketing fluff.

[12:03] Daniel Cho: Yeah, we did. Although we call it “prompt caching,” but same thing.

[12:07] Markus Klein: Yeah, same thing. Sometimes transcript tools call it “prompt cash” which is… not it.

[12:13] (crosstalk)

[12:14] Priya Shah: (laughs) Yeah.

[12:16] Avery Johnson: Alright. Since we’re aligned, can we treat this as a soft yes, pending seeing the consent form and confirming logo approval path?

[12:26] Priya Shah: Soft yes. I’m supportive.

[12:29] Daniel Cho: Yeah, I’m in.

[12:31] Camila Reyes: Amazing. I’ll send the consent form draft today. It’s not scary, but it’s legal-ish.

[12:38] Avery Johnson: And I’ll send a couple times for the interview. Priya, what’s your availability next week? Tuesday/Wednesday?

[12:45] Priya Shah: Tuesday afternoon could work. Wednesday morning maybe.

[12:50] Daniel Cho: I’m more free Wednesday.

[12:52] Avery Johnson: Okay. I’ll propose: Tuesday 2pm PT, Wednesday 10am PT, and Thursday 1pm PT. Something like that.

[13:01] Priya Shah: Sounds good.

[13:03] Markus Klein: For the architecture diagram, I’ll send a template. You can mark up what’s too detailed. We can keep it to like four boxes.

[13:12] Daniel Cho: Please.

[13:14] Camila Reyes: For metrics, maybe in the interview we capture: before/after p95, and any qualitative “we stopped paging for timeouts.” Even if it’s not a number.

[13:26] Priya Shah: We can do qualitative. For numbers, ranges only.

[13:30] Camila Reyes: Perfect.

[13:31] Avery Johnson: Awesome. While we’ve got you—anything you’d want the story to emphasize? Like, what do you want other engineering leaders to take away?

[13:41] Priya Shah: For me, it’s predictability. Hosted stuff was easy but we couldn’t control tail latency. Dedicated gave us control. And your team helped tune it quickly.

[13:54] Camila Reyes: That’s a great quote right there. (laughs)

[13:57] Priya Shah: (laughs) Yeah, we’ll see.

[14:00] Daniel Cho: I’d emphasize the tooling. The console breakdown helped us see where the cost was coming from. Like tokens vs overhead.

[14:08] Markus Klein: Love that. Token-level breakdown. Also the “per route” view.

[14:13] Daniel Cho: Yeah.

[14:14] Avery Johnson: Great. That maps exactly to our messaging pillars: performance economics, reliability, and operational tooling.

[14:22] Priya Shah: Just don’t overpromise. Like, we still do work on our side.

[14:26] Camila Reyes: 100%. We try to be very factual.

[14:29] Avery Johnson: Cool. Last thing—reference calls: would you prefer we do them with you, Priya, or Daniel, or rotate?

[14:37] Priya Shah: It depends. If it’s exec-to-exec, I can do. If it’s technical deep dive, Daniel or Alex.

[14:45] Markus Klein: We can match the audience. And we’ll keep calls to 30 minutes.

[14:50] Daniel Cho: And no recordings, please.

[14:53] Avery Johnson: Absolutely. We don’t record reference calls unless you explicitly opt in, which we won’t ask.

[14:59] Camila Reyes: And we’ll log internally that the call happened, but not details of what you said.

[15:06] Priya Shah: Good.

[15:08] Avery Johnson: Great. I think that’s it. Camila will send consent form, I’ll send scheduling, Markus will send diagram template.

[15:16] Camila Reyes: Yep.

[15:18] Markus Klein: Yep.

[15:19] Avery Johnson: Thanks again both. Talk soon.

[15:23] Priya Shah: Thanks.

[15:24] Daniel Cho: Thanks.

---
